newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy budget faces crunch after huge demonstration.
newsitem.headline: Italy budget faces crunch after huge demonstration.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government said on Sunday it was willing to negotiate with the centre-right after hundreds of thousands rallied against proposed tax hikes in the 1997 austerity budget it is pushing through parliament.

With just four days to go before the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) is due to vote on the budget bill, the biggest party in Prime Minister Romano Prodi's coalition proposed a review of the draft package for possible changes.

Massimo D'Alema, leader of the ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), made the comment after up to 500,000 Italians, far more than expected, flocked to an opposition march in Rome on Saturday to protest against the budget.

"We will look carefully at who has been demonstrating and see whether it is possible to correct, and where to correct, a finance bill which nevertheless for the first time does not hit the popular classes," he said.
Prodi said on Sunday he was willing to discuss budget details with opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi after the billionaire media mogul denounced his government at the rally as a shameful regime.
The rival blocs are deadlocked over special powers the government wants to set policy on sensitive budget areas, including tax, without the need for parliamentary approval.
Berlusconi has hinted that his Freedom Alliance bloc may hold hostage a plan for constitutional reform, which requires broad cross-party support, until Prodi gives ground.

"Either the fiscal powers are removed or no-one should expect a submissive opposition," hard-right leader Gianfranco Fini told the rally. "This here is a moderate Italy, but one that is on its feet and ready to fight."
D'Alema has championed discussions with Berlusconi on reform and political commentators said his olive branch on the budget appeared to be a concession to keep the talks alive.
Corriere della Sera newspaper said in an editorial it was now imperative to find out "quickly, from today, whether Prodi is willing to take a step backwards on the budget".
If not, it warned: "The road of understanding between the Freedom Alliance and (Prodi's) Olive Tree will be truly cut".

The Chamber of Deputies, where Prodi relies on the hardline Communist Refoundation for a majority, is due to hold its final vote on the budget on Thursday. Commentators say Prodi may have to use confidence votes to sweep away opposition filibustering.
The bill is then due to pass to the Senate, which Prodi controls. It must be passed by both houses by the year-end.

Saturday's demonstration, which culminated in Piazza San Giovanni, a traditional bastion of the left, was seen as a blow for Prodi as he struggles to sell hugely unpopular taxes to a discontented public.
His 1997 budget aims to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($42 billion) off next year's deficit to enable Italy to qualify for Europe's planned single currency.

One of its most contested elements is a one-off "Euro-tax", but details remain unclear. Many fear the extra cost, on top of some of the highest tax rates in western Europe, will not get Italy into Economic and Monetary Union anyway.
Many shopkeepers in Italy closed their doors and staged a day-long demonstration last week against planned tax hikes.
Prodi, lambasted by demonstrators as a lying Pinocchio who would even tax the air Italians breathe, remained calm.
"It is a big demonstration by a significant minority which represents real interests in the country," he said after the rally. "But we represent deeper and more widespread interests."
